issues.legal_issue: A person who continues in possession of agricultural land after the deemed lease term with the landlord’s consent retains tenant status and statutory protection against eviction based solely on expiry of the lease.
material_facts: The agricultural lease document was unregistered, so its stated fixed term could not be relied on to establish the lease’s duration.
The tenant remained in possession beyond the deemed lease period with the landlord’s consent; that consent ceased only when the landlord sought possession in the tenant’s injunction suit.
The landlord sought a mandatory injunction based on expiry of the lease, rather than eviction on a statutory ground and through the prescribed procedure.
issues.conclusion: The tenant’s continued possession with the landlord’s consent made him a tenant holding over and entitled to protection under the 1953 Act. Expiry of the lease alone did not entitle the landlord to evict him; the order against the tenant was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(6) and 9 of the Punjab Security of Land Tenure Act, 1953, read with Section 4(5) of the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, a tenant holding over with the landlord’s consent remains within the statutory protection against eviction except on the grounds specified in Section 9. Section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 gives legitimacy to possession continued with the landlord’s consent after expiry of the deemed lease term. Section 40 of the 1887 Act, which permits ejectment on expiry of a fixed term, does not override the protection provided by Section 9 of the 1953 Act; eviction must follow the procedure in Section 14-A. The court distinguished the position discussed in Sukhdev Singh (Dead) through Legal Representatives v. Puran, and relied on the holding-over principle in Section 116.

rule.if: agricultural_tenancy_status_dispute and unregistered_agricultural_lease and possession_continued_after_deemed_lease_term and landlord_consented_to_continued_possession and landlord_objected_only_after_continuance

predicates.agricultural_tenancy_status_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an occupant of agricultural land retains tenant status and protection against eviction.
predicates.unregistered_agricultural_lease: The parties’ agricultural lease document was not registered.
predicates.possession_continued_after_deemed_lease_: The occupant remained in possession after the lease term that could legally be established had elapsed.
predicates.landlord_consented_to_continued_possessi: The landlord permitted the occupant to remain in possession after that term elapsed.
predicates.landlord_objected_only_after_continuance: The landlord’s objection to the continued possession arose only after the occupant had remained in possession with consent.

issues.definition: When an occupant of agricultural land remains in possession beyond the legally established lease term with the landlord’s consent, the landlord cannot evict the occupant solely because that term has elapsed.

issues.legal_issue: The terms of an unregistered agricultural lease cannot establish a fixed duration where the governing registration requirements apply, and the lease is treated as running from year to year.
material_facts: The lease concerned agricultural land and was not registered.
The applicable notifications extended Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 to the relevant territory, while Section 117 of that Act had not been extended there.
The stated lease term was relied on to argue that the tenancy had ended, but the lease terms could not be considered to determine its duration.
issues.conclusion: The lease terms were inadmissible to determine the lease’s duration, and the agricultural lease was deemed to run from year to year under Section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17 and 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, read with Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, prevent the terms of an unregistered instrument from being used to establish the duration of a lease requiring registration. Although Section 117 of the Transfer of Property Act generally excludes agricultural leases from Chapter V, it had not been extended to the relevant territory; Section 107 therefore applied to agricultural leases there. In the absence of an admissible instrument establishing a different term, Section 106 treated the lease as running from year to year. Anthony v. K.C. Ittoop & Sons was distinguished because it concerned a non-agricultural lease governed by rent-control legislation.

predicates.agricultural_lease_duration_dispute: The parties dispute the duration of a lease of agricultural land.
predicates.lease_document_unregistered: The document recording the lease was not registered.
predicates.applicable_law_requires_registration_for: The law applicable to the dispute requires leases of the relevant duration to be made by a registered instrument.
predicates.agricultural_leases_are_not_exempt_from_: The governing law in the relevant territory does not exempt agricultural leases from the registration requirement.

issues.definition: If an agricultural lease document is unregistered and the applicable law requires registration without exempting agricultural leases, its terms cannot establish a fixed duration and the lease is treated as running from year to year.
